chunks.text: Hi everyone, now we are going to study our first data structure which is called arrays.
Now, in what situations do we use arrays?
Suppose we have to store marks of three subjects.
These three subjects can be physics, chemistry, and math.
Now, the simplest way to store marks of these three subjects is to make integer variables for these three.
First, we made an integer variable for physics, then for chemistry, and then for math.
And what we did is we stored our marks in these three.
Now, we are given a situation where we have to store marks of our college subjects.
In colleges, you have to study 5-6 new subjects every semester for 6 months.
So, you have to study so many subjects in 4 years that there is no count for them.
But let's keep a sample count here.
Suppose you have to store marks of 50 subjects.
Now, for these 50, you cannot create different integer variables because it will be difficult to track them.
Because no one will remember all the subjects.
So, in such a situation, we make a structure which looks like this.
And we call it arrays.
What will happen in arrays?
First, we will store marks of subject 1, then subject 2, then subject 3, then subject 4,
then subject 5.
And in this way, we will store marks of all 50 subjects in a single list.
So, it is a list type structure.
Now, we give some indexes to the positions in this.
For example, we give index 0 to the first position, index 1 to the second, index 2 to the third, and so on.
So, we will give index 49 to the 50th position.
So, we have made an array of 50 sizes from 0 to 49.
And we can store marks of 50 subjects in it.
Now, the most common question that students ask is why did we start with 0?
We could have started with 1.
So, this thing is called zero-based indexing.
That is, our index or position starts from 0.
Now, C++ or Java, these languages work on zero-based indexing.
So, things start from 0 here.
But if you explore some other languages, then indexing starts from 1 there.
But we have to remember that we are reading C++ and Java, so all types of indexing will always start from 0.
Now, first of all, let's understand what is the formal definition of an array?
If the interviewer or examiner asks you, then what do you have to write or tell there?
Array is a list of elements of the same type.
That is, an array is a list of elements where you store the same type of elements.
If you want to store apple, mango, 4.9, and 8.
You cannot make an array by combining these four because it has a type string.
This is also a string.
This is a floating value and this is an integer.
But if you only want to store marks or numbers,
or you just want to store strings like our fruits are called apple, mango,
or you want to store a floating variable like 1.1, 4.9, 8.6, 2.8.
For this, you can make an integer array.
For this, you can make an array of string type.
And for this, you can make an array of float type.
So, the same type of data should be stored in the arrays.
There will be strings in the string, int in the int, and float in the float.
Similarly, we will have to store characters in the character array.
Now, the definition is not only this, there is a second part in this.
Elements are stored in a contiguous memory location.
That is, our elements are stored one after another.
Now let's understand this.
You can imagine the memory of the computer like the earth.
Like people have cut a plot on the earth.
This plot is mine, this plot is yours.
We make our house on it.
We store things in it.
Similarly, we have the memory of our computer.
We visualize the memory of the computer in this way.
What do we do in this?
We cut our plot.
That is, we made this part, this part, this part, and this part.
And the size of each part is 1 byte in the computer.
The size of the unit of the memory of the computer is 1 byte.
And we can store 0 or 1 in it.
Now we know that the integer is 4 bytes.
So we make big boxes here that signify our integers.
Suppose this is 4 bytes.
This is also 4 bytes.
And this is also 4 bytes.
So if we make an array of 3 sizes.
What kind of an array?
An array in which we have stored 3 elements.
For example, our array will look like this.
In which this index will be 0, this index will be 1, and this index will be 2.
Here we will store our physics marks.
Here we will store our chemistry marks.
And here we will store our math marks.
So if we have to store all three of them in the memory, then how will we store them?
Here we will store our physics marks.
Here we will store our chemistry marks.
Here we will store our math marks.
So these memory locations are running one after the other.
For example, there is an address of every plot in the ground.
So that you can give things there and you can take things from there.
Similarly, there is an address of every location in the memory.
If its address is 1000, then its address will be 1004 and its address will be 1008.
How was this taken out?
We have taken anything of this, it has taken a random address.
Now we know that the next location is 4 bytes away.
Because the size of this location is 4 bytes.
So if we add 4 to this, then the next location will be 1004.
Now if we add 4 to the next location which is also 4 bytes away, then the next location will be 1008.
Similarly, if this was an area of 4 sizes, then we would have added 4 to this again and the next location would be 1012.
Now let's consider another example.
In this case, we make an area in which characters are stored.
So the size of our characters is equal to 1 byte.
Now we will store 3 characters.
In the first location, A is stored, in the second location, B is stored, and in the third location, C is stored.
This is 012 index.
We have named this area ABC.
Now how will ABC look in the memory?
In the ABC memory, something like this will look.
Where the first location will be A, its address is 1000.
So in the next location, B will be stored and the address of B will be 1001.
Because its size is equal to only 1 byte.
So we will add 1 to this.
When C is added, then the size of C will be 1002.
So in this way, our elements are stored on contiguous memory locations.
And this is a very important thing to understand that how the elements are stored in the array.
Now the most important thing in data structure is their visualization.
Why do we write the array in a straight line?
Because they are stored in the straight line in the memory.
Trees are not stored in a straight line.
That's why trees don't look straight like arrays.
Neither does stack store like arrays.
That's why stack is not made like this.
Stack is made one above another.
Because in that, we are visualizing things and memory on top of each other.
So these are very important things that why every structure looks the way it looks.
